faq.a: High in a cold cloud, water vapour freezes directly onto a tiny speck of dust or pollen, making a small six-sided ice crystal. It then grows as more vapour freezes onto it.
Water molecules are bent, and when they freeze they link with hydrogen bonds into rings of six. That six-sided pattern repeats through the whole crystal.
asks: Why does ice make six-sided shapes?

faq.a: The corners of a growing crystal stick out furthest into the moist air, so they gather water vapour fastest and shoot out into arms, which sprout side branches.

Every snowflake takes its own path through the cloud, meeting slightly different temperatures and moisture, so complex flakes are almost certainly all different. Very small, simple crystals can look nearly the same.

faq.q: Why is snow white if ice is clear?
faq.a: Snow is a jumble of countless tiny ice crystals with air between them. Their many surfaces bounce all colours of light back in every direction, which looks white.

facts: Wilson Bentley of Vermont photographed more than 5,000 snowflakes, starting in 1885.
Thin plates and star-shaped snow crystals grow near minus 15 degrees Celsius, while needles and columns grow near minus 5.

quiz.say: What decides whether a snow crystal grows into a star, a plate or a column?

options.show: The temperature and moisture of the air

options.say: How windy it is on the ground

quiz.why: Crystals grow differently at different temperatures and humidities: stars and plates near minus 15 degrees, needles and columns near minus 5.

wrong.1: Cloud colour depends on thickness and light, and does not shape the crystals.
wrong.2: The crystal grows high in the cloud, far from ground winds.
